utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. From a different environment, you can see that as envisaged, today this is not an ordinary hearing. This is a taken deposition under Rule 71, and today, I do not act in my capacity as presiding judge but as presiding officer under Rule 71 (A). Nevertheless, may we please hear in what case we are acting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the transcript, we need the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. And the complete Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Presiding officer. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any obstacles to start immediately with the hearing of today's witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We can begin. There was earlier this morning a technical problem with the video, but when we reach that point, we'll see if it has been solved yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. -- To be cautious, our witness has no protection, no pseudonym?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In open session. So may I ask the usher to escort Mr. Vulliamy into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's the intention to hear you as a witness in the framework of Rule 71 in order to take a deposition in the case Prosecutor versus Dr. Stakic. And may we please hear your solemn declaration, first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. And the floor is open for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask that the ELMO be moved out of the way for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell the Court, or the presiding officer, your name and your profession?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My full name is Edward Sebastian Vulliamy, and I'm a journalist, a reporter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you tell the -- for the purpose of this hearing, I'll be calling them Judges, don't worry about that, there's a technical difference because we are missing one judge but there's no reason for you to concern yourself with that. Can you tell the Judges what your background is as a journalist, in other words chronologically go through your various employment and positions from when you began working as a journalist until today's date.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. After finishing my studies, I joined a local paper in the west of England. After that, I went to work for a local news programme in Manchester in the north of England. I suppose it began when I was promoted to a programme called "World in Action" which is the main international current affairs programme on English, British independent television. That's to say not the BBC. I was there for five years working as a researcher, reporter. And that took me to many countries. I was -- I focussed on northern Ireland and the conflict there, covering it from all sides, the British, what is called the Protestant, the Catholic, republican. I also got to work on programmes in the Middle East, in Australia, Poland, Gdansk and the uprising. The United States and all across western Europe. I then decided that I wanted to write. Television wasn't really necessarily for me. And I went to join the Guardian newspaper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just ask you to fill in on that the year that you finished your studies and began your work as a journalist, and to the point that you decided to become a writer as opposed to working in television?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: You mean why?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, just the years.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. This is 1985. I joined the Guardian on the 1st of January, 1986. And I have been with that company ever since. The -- my duties initially were on the national desk, British news, but also features, arts, sport, general reporter. And occasionally working in western Europe as well. After some years, in 1989, they decided that in their wisdom, they wanted to make me an editor, and I was promoted to the position of editor of the newspaper's magazine. But after six months -- well, what happened is the Berlin wall came down, and I thought that editing wasn't quite my thing. I preferred to work in the field, and I sort of assigned myself to go to Berlin, and that was a bit of a turning point because that's when I went to the paper and said: "Look, I want to stay with this." And I did. I covered the fall of communism in eastern Europe. Romania being the main event that Christmas, the fall of Ceausescu, and the conflict across Romania at that time. I was then -- I wanted to stay in that arena, but -- and to join the foreign staff. And the vacancy they had was in Rome, so they posted me in 1990 in Italy where I set up a new office because they wanted to start covering southern Europe more seriously. And ironically, my brief was to cover southern Europe and Italy and to keep an eye on Yugoslavia, which in 1990 was not much in the headlines. Pardon me. But -- so I yes, I worked a lot on the corruption scandals that were breaking open in Italy at that time. But in the summer of 1991 was asked to go to Slovenia to examine the situation there, the Slovenes were making a bid for independence from Yugoslavia. And that led on to Croatia, and from the very beginnings of the -- what everyone wants to call it, the war of independence, between Croatia and the shrinking Yugoslavia, I covered that at what I could call close range. I was all across the various front lines of that country. So I suppose I had unwittingly and unintentionally become a war reporter, except I omitted to say in early 1991, before -- and forgive me if I regress chronologically, I was also dispatched by way of a sort of emergency coverage to Baghdad in the weeks immediately preceding and the weeks immediately following the Gulf war. We were thrown out of Iraq when the war started. And I was able to get back into Baghdad after the war and to work in Kurdistan and in the south of Iraq where I got, I suppose if you don't count Romania, my first taste of war while working for the newspaper. But to go back to Croatia, that conflict was, in its way, resolved in December 1991. I went back to working in Italy, but not long after, the war began or the conflict began in Bosnia. And perhaps a short of shorthand would help at this point. For the next two and a half years, two years, my time was spent between Bosnia-Herzegovina, which again I covered at I would say very close range indeed, and Italy, where I was trying to live, without much success. I then was -- early in 1994, spring 1994, was, sort of at the paper's insistence really, sent to the United States. They thought I needed a change, and I was made the bureau chief for the Observer newspaper in the United States. The Guardian had bought the Observer to be its Sunday edition, if you like. And I did that for about a year, but at my own request, returned to Europe to be based in London and to continue working on the, by now, concluding war in Bosnia. And I was then commissioned by my editor to do a long and fairly detailed retrospective series of articles which I did between roughly the signing of the Dayton agreement and the following summer on aspects of the war that it was felt hadn't been covered or known about during the day-to-day coverage. We called it "the Secret War". Now, I then returned to the United States. They gave me a second chance to go back to America, and I was posted once again in Washington with the same position, bureau chief for the U.S., for the Observer. I should, sorry, say when I was back in Europe I was working with the Guardian. But this was back with the Observer again. There was a fluid situation between the staff of both newspapers, then being part of the same group and indeed in the same building. And that's where I have been ever since. I moved to New York in 1999, but I've covered all aspects of the politics and social matters in the United States, from school shootings. I have been in Haiti a number of times. I have been in Nicaragua, Mexico, Jamaica, gang warfare. Unless you want a more complete list. I have been covering the Americas ever since. And, of course, the climax, I suppose you could say, was the morning of September the 11th last year when I was buying my coffee not far from the World Trade Centre when the towers came down. And that has obviously been the -- that and the war in Afghanistan have been the main preoccupation over the past year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, is it correct, Mr. Vulliamy, that you were one of the first group of foreign journalists to visit the Omarska camp in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was one of the first group to go into the camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- just setting the scene for that, can you go back and tell us how that trip began? What was the impetus that first led to you or your editors deciding to try to enter the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I had already reported from the Former Yugoslavia and was on the, if you like, the roster of journalists covering the by now shifted conflict into Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the background is specifically this: My newspaper, the Guardian, published -- well, the latest in a number of articles about reports of the Omarska camp. And this was based on -- mostly on word from refugees or deportees who were crossing from Bosnia into the Croatian city of Karlovac. On the same day as our main story was published, not by me but by a colleague of mine called O'Kane, another story was published in an American paper called Newsday by a Mr. Gutman. And it so happened that on that day, that very day, Radovan Karadzic, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, was in London for some conference or other. And he was on the ITN news that night, ITN being Independent Television News, the main independent, that is to say, non-BBC, news. And the gist of his argument was that these reports were untrue, they were fabrications, they were wrong. And he laid down a sort of challenge to the effect of: "Come and see for yourselves, if you insist." And in a nutshell, we did. I was involved because it was my turn to go back to Bosnia anyway. And it was -- the story had been in the guardian. So if you like, ITN and ourselves teamed up, and my boss, the foreign editor, whose name is Webster, spoke to Dr. Karadzic on his car phone, as I recall, on Dr. Karadzic's way to the airport and said: "Well, we are coming and our reporter is leaving immediately for Belgrade." ITN also went straight away, and I met up with them in Budapest actually because you couldn't fly to Belgrade. You had to go by car from Hungary. I think perhaps Dr. Karadzic anticipated a longer --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you not to speculate about Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Okay. So we went to Belgrade. And that's how it came about. We arrived expecting to go to Omarska directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Belgrade, do you recall what date that would have been?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I think it would have been the 28th or the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were also journalists from ITN television. Can you name them, who were accompanying you at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There were two. If I can explain. ITN is a news company which makes -- which makes the news for two different channels, Channel 3 and Channel 4. I suppose because of the gravity of this, they chose to send two television crews, one for Channel 3 and one for Channel 4. The reporter for Channel 3 news was called Penny Marshall, and for the Channel 4 news was called Ian Williams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Belgrade, did you speak to any officials from the Bosnian Serb entity at that time or from Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we were met by officials from the Serbian and the Bosnian Serbian authorities, and the main host from the Bosnian Serbs was the vice-president of their Republika Srpska whose name was Nikola Koljevic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a fluent English speaker. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: His English was very good, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a professor of literature of some kind?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's what I was told. He was a professor of English literature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, do you speak any foreign languages?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I speak fluent Italian and French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you not speak any languages of the Former Yugoslavia, that being Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian, or Albanian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I picked up a pidgin version over the period but I would certainly not claim to speak that language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were your discussions with Mr. Koljevic and the authorities from the Serbian Republic, that is, the Yugoslavian federal authorities, all dealing with your desire to go visit the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there was little else. Professor Koljevic said that we would get to Omarska but first of all arrangements had been made for us to visit other places. And I suppose you could say that a number of days of impatient conversations began when he made that proposition because we were not there to visit other places; we were there to visit Omarska. But the combination of Professor Koljevic and the federal Yugoslav authorities had organised various visits for us that they insisted we make to other centres, camps, places, which reluctantly because there were no other plans on offer, we undertook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't want to cover this in detail, but briefly did you cover various detention officers in Serbia and did you report that the -- that the conditions there were adequate or humanitarian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. In particular, a place called Loznica, which is right on the border of Bosnia, in fact you can see Bosnia from the place, it was a converted school, and the conditions were not good, but the conditions were not bad. And indeed, one wondered why we were there. It was by no means anything worth the kind of language that had been used to describe Omarska. By no means. It was not bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just briefly, though, is it correct that you had received reports from the other side, to call it that, the government in Sarajevo or some people there, that these camps were -- did have inhumane conditions and you determined that there was no evidence of that from your journey. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I had seen it -- sorry, I had not seen it. But there was a list, and I don't know whether Loznica was on that list. But I know that government in Sarajevo was saying that the conditions were inhumane in the federal republic, and if Loznica was on that list, they were certainly wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Proceeding now, from Belgrade, where did you travel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We messed around or got messed around in Belgrade for a number of days. And on the 3rd of August, we were flown by helicopter, by federal army helicopter, to Pale, which was the sort of ad hoc capital of the Serbian bit of Bosnia outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Pale, did you again have an opportunity to speak yourself with Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we were greeted by Dr. Karadzic, and we were taken immediately to his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the conversation with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, obviously we were pushing to go to Omarska, and that was -- when are we going? And he said: "I promise you will go to Omarska Omarska," and he reiterated his authority for that visit. But he said that -- well, he said a number of things. He said first of all that he wanted us to see some more places where Muslims were being held before we went there, in the immediate vicinity. He said that he hoped we would also make efforts to visit camps on the other side where Serbs were being held. And gave us some advice as to where we might try. And he went on to warn us that he couldn't guarantee for our safety during our trip to Omarska. He said that the -- that journalists were being targeted by the Muslims and the result of their attacks being blamed on the Serbs, and that we should be wary of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, visit any Serbian-controlled camps in the Pale area before departing Pale?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. Again, reluctantly, because we wanted to get on. But yes, we did. We went to visit -- or were taken to visit a camp at a place called Kula.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the conditions that you observed during your visit at Kula?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sad. My conclusion was -- or my inference was that this was a centre where men and a few women were being kept for exchange, human currency for prisoners on the other side or captives on the other side. And it was a reasonably well-run place actually. It was sad. It was not pleasant, and a couple of the people there talked about beatings, but we saw no evidence of them. And the conditions were not that bad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Pale, where did you travel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We stayed overnight in Pale, and went by road the following day, which would be the 4th of August, on a long drive, long by necessity of not crossing front lines and so on, the place was obviously a crisscross of territory. So we drove in a convoy, a vehicle, a military vehicle, or were driven in a military vehicle from Pale north through the east of Bosnia to a town called Bijeljina. And from there west through what was called the corridor, a narrow corridor of Serbian-controlled territory, between Croatia and the northern government-controlled area to Banja Luka, through Brcko, a very badly damaged town with some quite shocking damage, shell and -- shell fire and mortar fire damage. Deserted. And then on to Banja Luka, the biggest city in the Krajina area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, did you meet with various officials in an official capacity regarding your proposed trip to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The following morning, yes, after a rather unpleasant reception we met with a man called Major Milutinovic. He was the representative of the military authorities in Banja Luka, and he met up with us the following morning. That would be the 5th of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, did you see Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Professor Koljevic actually sort of bobbed up all over the place. He was in Pale when we got there. And he was in Bijeljina when we got there. Joined us for lunch. And I think he was in Banja Luka as well. I don't remember having a long conversation with him in Banja Luka, but he was there, and that's where he bade us farewell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry, he was there in the evening but not the following morning when we met Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following morning, which was I believe you indicated was the 5th of August, can you tell us where you travelled that day?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We drove with Major Milutinovic from Banja Luka west towards Prijedor. And what I remember best from the journey was driving past the southern edges of a town which I now know to be the town of Kozarac where the damage was very extensive, almost all the houses had been burned or shelled, with one or two left remaining intact with their occupants still tending their gardens or small agricultural property. And Major Milutinovic told us that these remaining inhabitants were the local Serbian population and that he gave us a figure of some 40.000 Muslims which he said had decided to leave the area, and he gave us a history of the area. But that's where we drove. And we arrived then in Prijedor, which is a little further on. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I presume that Major Milutinovic is your official escort at this time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have your own vehicles or were you travelling in military vehicles or did you have any military or police escorts?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: At some point, an -- we had gone from Pale to Banja Luka in a military sort of van thing. At some point, an ITN vehicle hooked up with this, which they had ordered from Belgrade. I don't remember when that arrived actually, but we were travelling in -- I think Major Milutinovic's car at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Prijedor, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We arrived in the city -- in the town and went straight to the civic centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told who you were going to meet with? Do you remember now whether or not Major Milutinovic had told you what the purpose of going to the centre of town was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I don't remember what he told us, but I remember what we told him. We said we wanted to meet the people who were going to give us the authority to go to Omarska. That's why we're here. I should perhaps say that by now, we were pressing as hard as we possibly could and patience was getting pretty thing, because it was clear, and I'm not going to infer -- it was clear we were being messed about. We had been delayed and delayed. And he -- maybe he said something. "I will take you to the people or this is the next stage of your trip." But we certainly made it clear to him that we hoped whoever was in this office were the people who were going to fulfill Dr. Karadzic's guarantee to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to that building, what happened?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We went in and we were greeted on the ground floor, in the entrance, by a man who was introduced as the chief of the police. His name, Simo Drljaca. And we were then taken upstairs to a sort of conference room and introduced to another group of men who were -- who we were told were called the crisis committee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall - and obviously you've seen videos of that since that time --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the individuals who were present at that table, representing the authorities from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Indeed. They were the mayor, the top official, Milomir Stakic; his deputy, Milan Kovacevic; the man who we were given to believe was the top military man in the area, a Colonel Vladimir Arsic; Mr. Drljaca was already with us, by then having come up the stairs. And there was a lady, a Mrs. Nada Balaban or Ms. Nada Balaban. And there were other people in the room to whom we were not introduced by name and milling about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. You mentioned, transcript page 14, line 17, "crisis committee." Quite sure, to the best of your recollection, that they were called indeed "crisis committee" or could it be the notion was "Crisis Staff" or "Municipal Assembly" or something else in this direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Crisis Staff, possibly. Municipal Assembly, that would certainly surprise me. Crisis Staff, maybe. But Municipal Assembly, I think not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, crisis committee versus crisis staff, what have the notion, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If it's Crisis Staff, I stand corrected, and that would not surprise me. But Municipal Assembly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, it would be appropriate to clarify. Were you using interpreters during these exchanges with the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was interpreting for you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was variously a man who was hired by ITN as a translator, and Ms. Balaban who was, I think, their translator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without going into names, is it correct that the normal policy would be always to use a local interpreter from the area rather than bringing one from Sarajevo, for example?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that your practice covering the wars in the Former Yugoslavia would be to use a local interpreter from the area in which you were working at that time rather than bringing an interpreter across lines to the other side?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, this gentleman who was in the employ or hired by ITN was not actually local to the area. He was from Belgrade. But certainly you would not want to have anybody from the other side working with you on the other side because that would be very unsafe, I think, for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So perhaps -- did ITN, to your knowledge, record at least part of the meeting with the members of what you called the crisis committee?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, I doubt -- yeah. I doubt they'd have filmed all of it, because it was quite a long meeting, but they would have filmed a bit of it. In fact, I know they did. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Did you have authority to tell the cameraman -- did you tell the cameraman turn your camera on or off? Did you do any of that producing or directing? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Absolutely not. We were there together because we were -- because in London, we had been entwined by the unfolding events. But I had absolutely no part of their journalistic enterprise, no, not at all. I was just doing my thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a mere print journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: A mere print journalist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us how many camera crews were there recording the event?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have said this before, or not. There were the two crews from ITN, and there was another film crew who had joined us in Pale. They were introduced to us the night before we left, therefore, the night of the 3rd of August. And they were from Bosnian Serb television, and they were making a film about us. And they were there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who was the first, to the best of your recollection now, ten years later, who were the first individuals to speak to you from the authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There were brief introductory remarks, I think from all of them, but certainly from Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic. The first -- once we -- once the sort of -- once the meaty discussion started, the first person we spoke to who spoke at length was Colonel Arsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Colonel Arsic say, to the best of your recollection now, regarding your plans to visit Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I remember very well what he said. Colonel Arsic recommended that we visit another place called Manjaca and said that we could go there almost straight away if we wanted to. And he said that Manjaca was under his authority and that we had his permission to go there. And we said, and I said, but the ITN people, too, through the interpreter, "no, we don't want to go to Manjaca, we want to go to Omarska. And that's what we are here for. And that's what Dr. Karadzic said we could do." And this went on for a good while. During which the more, and by now also the others joining in, said that it would be a good idea for us to go to Manjaca. We realised that Omarska was the place to go. I should perhaps that there were other motives. Manjaca had already been visited by the International Red Cross and deemed to be pretty bad. They were fairly shocked by what they found. So that was a, if you like journalistic reason not to go there. And if you forgive me, there was a purely journalistic reason not to go there, because a picture of Manjaca had already appeared in the papers, and I had reason to believe that the opposition, if you can call them that, Mr. Gutman, was about to go there himself. And we had a feeling that Omarska was the place to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the person then that did most of the talking at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Who did most of the talking? Most of the talking was Mr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall -- perhaps instead of asking you to recollect it, if the video is ready, I see it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we can put in the video. I don't believe it has been marked yet. It's on the 65 ter list as -- sorry, it is marked. It's S157. And sir, we're going to play this video. If you need to stop and comment, we can do that. Or we can go back. I think it's about 6 or 7 minutes long, and you can comment later. We do have a transcript of this to hand out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While that's being done, Mr. Vulliamy, so that no one is misled, this video is about 7 minutes long, how long is the meeting that you had?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Couple of hours, between an hour and a half and a couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what we're seeing is a small portion of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have some problems. This is public session, and we have visitors in the public gallery. And once again, it's their right to follow the proceedings. And what about the parties? May I first hear the observations by the parties as regards, yes -- it could be called infringement of the principle of public hearing. Please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not asking for it to be closed. I'm not sure I understand. We propose to play it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, but the principle of a public hearing includes, no doubt, that also the public gallery can following our proceedings. We'll say, to see the video. And we have visitors in the public galleries which are not able to follow the proceedings. How can we resolve this problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How have we done it in the past?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The last time the visitors in the public galleries waived the right to see the parts of the video. May I have observations by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll proceed in any manner the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can I understand that for these purposes, the Defence has no objections that it's not transmitted to the public gallery, and they will never, from this point or based on this point, any kind of objection or appeal?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That would be accurate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And I can see the visitors do not object that we proceed this way. Thank you. May we then start the video, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Journalist: That we could see Omarska and Trnopolje. "The Speaker: First, you are welcome. "The Journalist: Thank you. "The Speaker: Even if we have negative experience with the international press. "The Speaker: In the purpose of this, I would like you to show this very objective, not in the purpose of propaganda. "The Speaker: Two things that I do not agree with your visit here... "The Speaker: First is negative experience with the press. "The Speaker: Second is because you take a risk on your lives because you are in the war area."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just stop for a moment, please. Mr. Vulliamy, could you please be so kind and describe to the best of your recollections the person sitting there around there the desk. If we can see the still please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On our left is the mayor, Milomir Stakic. The gentleman who has been talking with the T-shirt is his number two, his deputy, Milan Kovacevic. And next to him is Colonel Arsic, and at the end next to the lady is the chief of police, Simo Drljaca. And that's Ms. Balaban in the pink blouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's not quite clear, at least on my screen, Dr. Stakic, did he wear civil clothes or was it a kind of uniform or even a camouflaged uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I shouldn't depend on my recollections. That wouldn't be right because I can see the film. But it seems to me to be military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could continue playing the tape a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Interpreter: If you have time to see one film here, what we prepared, that you better understand the situation here. Now we can talk about that what you want. "The Journalist: Okay, first this. "The Interpreter: First of all, we know very well what are the concentration camps. "The Interpreter: And we know better that than the English people. "The Interpreter: Because the -- in Britain, they, they have heard about that concentration camp, but they didn't believe it until 1943 or 1945. "The Interpreter: But we, we know that concentration camps and many of the people passed through that camps already in the Second World War. "The Interpreter: And you will see that there exists not any concentration camp here. And not 30, only... "The Interpreter: There's no concentration camp. There is some transit, transit camps... "The Interpreter: That you're going to see. "The Interpreter: He is glad that you are coming, come here to see this situation here, and from some other press media, another team. "The Interpreter: ... More and heavier clash than now. Even now we have some clashes around. He'd like to ask you, have you ever been to some other camp on other side where are the Serbs imprisoned. "The Journalist: I personally have not. "The Interpreter: Just want to say that they're simply glad, these people on their homes..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, first, again, did you have anything to do with the production or editing of the tape, the portion of the meeting, that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the transcript, which you don't have which the parties have, of that short clip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just note that the transcript, the person that was identified by the witness as Mr. Kovacevic is identified in the transcript as the president, and the male voice at the end was Dr. Stakic speaking where in the transcript it indicates "male voice." And we'll seek a correction on the official transcript. This is a draft.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the short clip we saw, there was some talk about a film being shown. Was a film, in fact, shown to you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: During the meeting?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, they showed us a video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that a video of?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was a video which they said supported their version of events that there had been what they called a jihad or an uprising by Muslims in the area, and I don't remember much about it. I was getting really annoyed by the time they put it on. But I do remember seeing some -- the great play made of people finding a copy of the Koran in a house, and I remember a shot of some soldiers opening up a box of sort of -- a machine-gun -- a strip of machine-gun bullets and various weapons being found and lots of pictures of soldiers, their soldiers, Bosnian Serb soldiers. But I don't remember much about it, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicated, and perhaps I missed something. You indicated that Colonel Arsic encouraged you to go to Manjaca. How was that finally resolved?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I mean, it wasn't resolved. It was resolved by us refusing to go to Manjaca and saying that that's not where we were going to go. Then he said: "If you want to go to Omarska, these are the people that you need to talk to."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just made a gesture to your right. Is that what Colonel Arsic did? Was that a gesture he made or explain what you meant?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He made a gesture. I don't remember whether he said it by name, but he gestured towards Mr. Kovacevic and Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any other recollection of anything that Dr. Stakic said during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: He gave a history of the events in the area in the immediate past. He talked about the discovery of weapons in the town of Kozarac. He specified 3.500 guns had been found. He said that the Muslims had been putting up barricades in the area on the roads. And he gave us some description of what sort of prisoners were kept in which, what he called, transit centres. And to summarise, I do have a note of this, not with me now. But to summarise, it was that Manjaca was those who had been arrested or captured in the Muslim militia, and Omarska and Trnopolje why civilians who were seeking to leave or wanting to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, were you taking a type of shorthand notes during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe we have copies of those. If at any time during your testimony you require them, please let us know. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And likewise the Court. I would be quite happy to read those any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May they be distributed immediately to the parties and the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, there's a small technical problem in that the actual copies we have are a sealed exhibit. The witness apparently -- I need to check one thing with him. I think the witness doesn't have an objection except I don't know if the names and phone numbers have been removed from these copies or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there's no sensitive material on those pages. So it's fine by me if -- I mean, perhaps I should have a look. But as -- I mean it would be okay by me if they help the Court. Then it's fine for them to be put into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you could review it first. Specifically, there was an order by Judge May to keep those under seal dated 18th of January, 2001, and I just realised that over the weekend. We don't have a problem with releasing it and neither does the witness, provided he does review and ensure that -- Mr. Usher, please, the witness should get them first and review them before even the registry. Yes. I would also warn the Court that I don't believe much is legible. It's in a shorthand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got something else here. I've got one page of shorthand, and something that isn't -- doesn't appear to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I believe the other materials are with the Registrar. You can hand everything to the witness, and he will look for his 1992 notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps that one is... These are the pages, Your Honour. No, these are fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They could be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Even if they should be marked under seal, or were marked under seal, now it's open material for the participants. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think I have the power to say that, Your Honour, since it's under seal. But I would indicate to the Court that these are copies of Mr. -- Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's the right of the witness, and if it's his assessment that there is no special protection needed, it may be open material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I see Mr. Vulliamy, these are going to be handed over to the Defence, and the accused has a right to look at those also.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. I have been handed by the Registrar. There are three pages of shorthand notes that were relevant in this, and I was handed about 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you only reviewed the pages related to 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: My understanding is that I'm being asked to enter on to the record the pages of shorthand I took pertaining to the notes in 1992 and Mr. Stakic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was shown by the Registrar a whole lot of other stuff. And I separated out those three pages, but I see that rather more than three pages has crossed the courtroom. In other words, material has been handed out that quite apart from that I am talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So no doubt, the order of Judge May still remains in power, save the three pages you just mentioned. They are, as far as I can understand you, open and no protection is needed, the three pages. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I can. The witness has indicated that we handed out a bunch of pages, that he doesn't know what else the Defence has been handed, and some of them maybe his personal notes that he has not yet consented to have released. He has only consented to have three pages released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we please proceed this way, the usher please take back to the OTP the other pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And if Mr. Vulliamy could identify to the usher the three pages that we're dealing with right now, we'll make sure the Defence and Court has those three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to do that, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have the three pages of notes now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please, now, have also for the Defence and the Judges one copy of these three pages in order to following the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could we borrow your three pages because my case manager is having trouble identifying what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may be heard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Quite frankly, we have an objection to the proceedings as how they're -- or actually, the process that the OTP is trying to attempt here with this witness. The witness has certainly kept notes of meetings that he has had in 1992 as well as 1996. In the prior trial where this witness has testified, Judge May, since he has been cited in terms of holding some of this evidence confidential, has certainly allowed in the other case to give the Defence in its entirety Mr. Vulliamy's handwritten, typed written, and I think as he called it, by a journalistic definition, a hybrid of those two so we could analyse it. I don't think it's necessary to wait until the eve of our cross-examination for the OTP to give that to us. Those documents, even though perhaps mistakenly given to us, should be given to us. And we insist that we get those at the earliest moment in time since Judge May has previously ruled that they are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No question about this. The purpose of this exercise is only to make a distinction between those three pages being public now and no longer under seal, and the other remaining pages, no doubt, they have been to be disclosed to you and no doubt, the Judges are more than eager to see these additional pages only for the purposes of this distinction public and under seal. Only for this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then they will be marked with different numbers. Provisional Exhibit Numbers. And when we are ready just to go to this procedure, as the admission of evidence will be done by the entire Trial Chamber, these documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could be heard on that, I guess I object to the handwritten notes being marked as an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I please, may I please proceed with that what I wanted to say. That for the purposes of the record, we already obtained a draft translation, and we expect later on a complete translation of that what we saw as videoevidence. No doubt, this video was already earlier during the hearing admitted into evidence as S157. For the purposes that we don't forget to admit later or not admit later the one or other document, we start today with a new collection of numbers. And this transcript of the video will be D1, (provisional S157-1). Then it will follow, will be followed by the next three pages being public now, tendered and provisionally marked as D2 (S -- and may I please have, Madam Registrar, the next available number for the hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S328. (S328). Decision on the admission into evidence will be done as soon as possible by the Chamber. There were additional remarks by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, my remark was just going to be that I don't have a problem with the witness referring and even reading that for the record, but to mark it as an exhibit to be translated is going to create tremendous problems since it's in a hybrid type of shorthand. It's basically not -- I don't know where we're going to find someone who can read it and translate it into the three languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For this purpose, can you please be so kind, we need this for the purposes for forensic purposes in this original version. But as you have noticed, in doubt, it would be problematic to have an interpretation of your shorthand. May I therefore ask you, for the purposes of the transcript and later, the hearings, that you could read what your notes are, the three pages you have before you. I would appreciate very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You can -- I think the question dealt with what Dr. Stakic said at the meeting, if you have any notes regarding Dr. Stakic said at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, there's a section that begins at the top of the page queued by the word "president Stakic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Respectfully, I don't agree with this proposal, if we admit these entire documents, also for the purpose of balancing who, say, took the lead during the conversation, I would ask you to read out everything we can read from this document. These three pages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. [As read] Chief of police, commandant: Colonel Arsic, region Vladimir, Manjaca, Manjaca. T-shirt. Pres. Of commune, Milomir Stakic. Kovacevic, vice-pres., exec. Of commune. Kovacevic: Even we had negative exp. with the int. press. In the papers of these, I want look you show these in obj., not for propaganda. I this not agree, negative exp. With the press. And secondly, because you can risk your lives because you are in the war area. What I suggest if you have. You are knowing what is a concentration, conc. camp. We know, but then the English people, because Britain, they have heard about conc. camps, but they didn't believe until 1943 to 45. But we know what conc. camps are, and many of us passed through conc. camps in the Second World War. "And you will see that there is not conc. camps here. There are transit camps that you are going to see. "President Stakic: I am glad you have come here to see this situation here. But I am sorry because the international publicity was not -- or publications, pub, was not int. two to three months ago in this area. At that time, there was heavier fighting than now. Two years ago, elections. There was -- government was half/half Serbians and Muslims. I was negotiating two sides, Serbs and the Muslims. Get try to agree, the others side to live in peace together. What we are looking for today. We think we have problems from the Muslim extremists here, not with the Muslim population. We asked the Muslims not to leave this area, but to live together with us. Serbs are not doing any genocide to other people. "We cannot make a nation. It is very difficult for such a country to exist. The other side buying weapons all the time. Croatian and Muslim extremists. We have a doc, a Kozarski. There are -- there were 3.500 armed people. We have the names and the weapons they have got. We have two tapes and by the Muslims how they were prepared for this war. Even we try very hard to not. They started to kill the Serbian people in this area. They made barricades. Beginning of May, on the main and side roads. Green headbands and berets. SDA, with a line through, Serbian people saw what was going to be and know what was in the Second World War. Started to protect themselves, their houses, in this area. We defend us from the first. A clash from other side. In that documentation, from all that we saw, from papers and documents, we had a fear what could be done to us. There's no conc. camps exists, only transit camps, that we put some of the refugees in their camps to protect them. And some come by themselves. The refugees who want to leave this area. Some of them want to go back to Bosnia, Izetbegovic country. And it is provided for most of them to go there, but there is many of the Muslim people, they don't want to go and live in that country. They want to go to Croatia, Austria, Germany. Now we are negotiate with UNPROFOR, and Int. Cross to provide those people with all the docs. Queueing to get the documents to go abroad. "Manjaca, arrow, those ones who are captured with weapons are investig. in army prison. Up at the top, Om. - Trn. All the rest are treated as civilian refugees. So the soldiers are in prison and will be investig. and tried. The others go into the transit camps. Omarska and Turn transit. About 2.000. Three to four thousand people, they want to leave there, have waiting to leave this area and does the other side, is there a Muslim. We are trying to stop. In the margin, Kovacevic, Milan, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. with lines indicating either this line or the following one. We are trying to stop some people, but other side say they didn't want. Ibeg. Swapped people. Ibeg. or Eebeg. swapped people to exchange Serbs. They ask a certain amount of flour, munitions and weapons. He doesn't want the people. These are not our prisoners. Babies down the river Una, crosses with their eyes gouged out. There is no -- there is not -- there is no our prisons. All are in the -- divided women and children. Then within the men, we investigate. Some from home. There are still some groups are still fighting. 18 groups don't want to give up. Yesterday, we had Muslim killed a soldier. Yet. One man of the SDA party came into the camp to be collected. Killed 20 Serbs. And soldiers, Hambarine. Mullah had from weapons all over from Hambarine on a list. Mosque used for. Three months began. I was born 41. Map. Born in Jasenovac. Propaganda video. Prisoner, he was preparing for war. Muslims accumulate medical supplies, transportation to their places."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May, Madam Registrar, please point out that this document, for the purposes of this deposition called D2, can be found on today's transcript from page 30, line 16 to page 33, line 5. It is time now for having a break. We will proceed at 11.30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Just for the record, no doubt it would be advantageous to call the provisional exhibits not as D exhibits but DP exhibits, which stands for deposition exhibits. So please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, after speaking with the authorities in the building at the municipal building, did they reach a final decision in your presence regarding your -- consent for your visit to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: -- Good while, discussion of maps and other things. And it got, I would say, fairly acrimonious. And after a while, we were told indeed to leave the room and the building and to go and wait outside by the vehicles while they attended to business and to our requests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For what length of period were you waiting outside?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I would say about 20 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that 20 minutes, was there anything notable that you observed in front of that municipal building?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, yes, and if I should have said before, I apologise. We had already noticed a long line of women waiting outside the building opposite the -- right across the road from the civic centre, which we were given to understand was the police station. And they were lined up along the sidewalk, and we, of course, saw them again when we went out, to wait outside, as instructed. And -- rather than just stand about, it seemed the obvious thing to do to go and talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did these women tell you in their conversations with them while waiting for a decision?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In a distressed manner, they said, almost unanimously, that they had come to the police station in search of information on their menfolk who had been taken away or vanished in one way or other. And they were looking for information about their husbands or sons, and we heard mention of Omarska quite a bit during the conversations we had with those women. I conducted a couple of interviews myself, as did the television crew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have been cautioned earlier today to pause before asking you the next question, so that would be why I'm pausing. Sir, were you able to determine the ethnicity of these women in the line?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After -- by the way, we have been talking about requesting to go to Omarska, did you mention to the authorities any other camp that you wished to view?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: ITN were particularly keen also on another place called Trnopolje. This had also been reported in the Guardian. I was anxious to see it, too. But for my specific, I mean, I talked about Omarska more than Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After 20 minutes or so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Mr. Drljaca and a dispatch of uniformed men came out of the civic centre and said we were going to Omarska after all. And they evicted a colleague of mine, a fellow I knew from before from a rival newspaper who had joined the convoy. They asked him if he was part of Dr. Karadzic's party? He admitted that he was not. And I confess to my professional relief, he was thrown off the convoy. So then we made to leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, this colleague, was he Mr. Juda, and he had come along just that day while you were waiting outside the municipal building, at that time had he come along and asked to join your group?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. If the Court will forgive professional considerations, he and a French journalists sort of arrived in a car and after all sort of efforts and time and delay, I was rather fed up to see him breeze down from Zagreb to say: "Oh, Omarska, great. We'll come, too." But he was not allowed to join th convoy because he wasn't part of what they called "Dr. Karadzic's party." And his name was, yes, Tim Juda from the Times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it that told Mr. Juda that he could not join your party?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was Major Milutinovic, but the conversations were had by some other people who were from Mr. Drljaca's dispatch. I should -- sorry, I should have said that Mr. -- Major Milutinovic also came out of the building with Mr. Drljaca at the end of that wait outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at that time, did you go to Omarska with Mr. Drljaca and Major Milutinovic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we set off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, did you notice anything during that journey to Omarska, anything along the roads that you passed?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We were not in the same vehicle as M same -- Mr. Drljaca. We were with Major Milutinovic. Yes, certainly noticed things. The burned out houses along the road, and then we, to my worry, we drove passed a sign off the main road saying "Omarska." And carried on, and then we turned off down a series of unpaved roads or very small or unpaved roads and through a sort of maze of lanes or minor roads. And there were houses either burned out, shelled, and deserted, or there were houses with white -- I saw flags, but they weren't flags, they were bits of sheeting or towelling or white textile hanging from trees or from windows. And we discussed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said you went past a sign for the Omarska camp. Between passing that sign and actually arriving in the camp, did something happen that delayed the journey again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah. While we were still driving this lot of minor roads, there was a burst of gunfire from the woods over our heads. And we were told to sort of duck, and some of the Serbian, they were uniformed -- they were in blue paramilitary uniforms, got out of an APC, a blue APC, armoured personnel carrier, and returned fire from a ditch. And there was a sort of minor, I wouldn't say battle, but exchange of fire, quite loud. And we were told that this was a mujahedin, Muslim extremists hiding in the woods attacking our convoy. I was, by now, in a very bad mood and very anxious to get to the camp. And I had also -- was not convinced in my mind that there were any so-called mujahedin in the area. And while some of our party were quite alarmed by this, I was, perhaps ill-advisedly, impatient and said something to Major Milutinovic to the effect that this is silly, let's just carry on, I'm not convinced -- let's just carry on. And the battle abruptly stopped, and we proceeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, this is August 5th, 1992, had you seen battle scenes, real battle scenes, in Bosnia? Had you been exposed to fire before that date?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Most certainly. I had seen exchanges of -- well, more than exchanges of fire in Croatia for several months, and I had been in Sarajevo prior to that which was not exactly -- about you I wouldn't describe as battles. But in Croatia I had certainly seen exchanges of fire and elsewhere, and in the West Bank, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything about the scene that you observed where the men jumped out of the APC and fired from a ditch that made you think that this was not an authentic battle, that this was staged?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, it didn't convince -- it was all much too overdramatic, and all the fire was coming over our heads in exactly the same place. I mean, if you're under fire, the fire is coming at you behind, in front, over. And it's -- I wasn't convinced. It was coming straight over our heads, and it was the way in which these guys with sunglasses jumped out of the APC. They were returning fire, they were aiming fairly high. It didn't feel right. It didn't feel convincing. I thought to myself then and I think now it was an attempt to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you indicated that you wanted to proceed, you said the battle stopped, and then did you go to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp, can you tell us from which part of the camp you arrived and what your first impressions were?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We arrived through what appeared to be a back gate. Inasmuch as there was no guard house or anything like that, and we came in. There were a series of red brick buildings around us. And in front, immediately in front -- I mean, ahead of us, a large red rust-coloured hangar or large warehouse building, and we went through the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: First, we were sort of marshalled and assembled in a yard, a tarmac yard, opposite the large hangar. I can't remember what was said because of what I saw, which was the rather extraordinary and unforgettable sight of a group of men, some 30 or so men, coming out of a door into the sunlight, out of the hangar, being lined up, and marshalled to order, and being made to run, drilled, across the yard in single file. And I remember seeing up above to my left, atop a building a sort of glass area or turret of some kind a man with a machine-gun watching them as they were drilled across the yard. And some of them were in what I would call reasonable seeming condition physically, but others were in a shocking condition. Near skeletal. A couple of them had shaven heads, extremely thin. And that, one could see even from the distance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened them -- then?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They were drilled across, and they went into a building on our left. And we were told to follow them, and we were told that this was the canteen. And we saw them line up for their midday meal in various states of decay. And they were given each a bowl of sort of watery stew soup. And either half or whole roll of bread. And they went to -- variously to the tables laid out in the room and started to eat their soup in a way that suggested quite honestly -- well, they looked like they were famished, and they started to attack this soup. And I got the impression they hadn't eaten for a long time. And we were told we could interview them, but it wasn't a very -- wasn't a very -- wasn't a situation where one felt able to interview them quite honestly. The guards were sort of mooching around, swinging their guns, and these men looked terrified.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see obvious injuries, any bruising or wounds on the people that you saw running across the yard and in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I couldn't see any wounds while they were running across the yard but there was a man with a wound to the side of his face. And I asked him through the interpreter what had happened, and he said that he had fallen over. And that was the gist of the conversations that we were having. If I can say this: That it was what they weren't saying that spoke a lot louder than what they were saying. There is something about the eyes of someone who is trying to communicate something to you that you know they can't communicate, and that was certainly the case. And certainly with regard to this man. You know, their eyes kind of burn. It's quite impressionable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This man that told you he fell down, did you ever see him again?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In rather strange circumstances. In the summer of 1995, I was -- well, I was above the town in Central Bosnia called Donja Vakuf with the by then advancing Bosnian army, and a sniper was shooting in a trench. And we were running along, got to a commander's hut. And this man said to me: "You were in Omarska, weren't you?" And I said: "Yes." And he said: "Do you remember me?" And I didn't actually because he had put on an awful lot of weight by then. Not put on weight, he had recovered weight. And he said: "Do you remember the man who said he had fallen over. And that was me. And I hadn't fallen over. That wound was inflicted." And that was quite a moment, I must say. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you introduced to the commander of the camp during your visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we were. Again, forgive me for not saying that earlier. That was before we went into the yard, before going into the canteen, we were introduced to the commander by the name of Meakic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many groups were you able to see come into the kitchen and eat?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The shift was a minute. You had a minute to eat your soup. And then they lined up and I noticed that some of them were keeping their roll or half a roll for later. So we would have seen I think two, if not three, shifts in their entirety, the first one, then there was a change. Then there was another change. So I think I would say three, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you request permission to see other parts of the camp decides the kitchen and the outdoor area that you saw?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, yeah. Certainly, because we wanted to get into the hangar because that was where the men had come from and we wanted to see what I was calling the sleeping quarters or the living quarters. And we asked -- in fact, that's why we spent perhaps less time in the canteen than we should have done because we were saying, let's move, let's move on from here. Let's look at the conditions as it were, you know, from which these men come to eat in this state that they were in. So we wanted to get into the hangar. And there were other buildings. You could other buildings quite clearly in the immediate vicinity of this yard. My understanding certainly from Dr. Karadzic's guarantee and the fact that back in Prijedor, we had been told that we were going to Omarska, that this was going to be a reasonably thorough inspection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever given permission to see the areas where the prisoners were kept or slept during that visit to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, we were taken upstairs for a long - forgive me - and pretty irrelevant briefing which went on and on. And actually, during that, there was another burst of gunfire in the woods and they said, oh, it's the mujahedin again. But I paid no heed whatsoever to that. The Bosnian Serb television crew were very excited by, it but we weren't. We were listening to these lectures and talked about various categories of prisoner, but we wanted to get on and look at the rest of the camp. But the briefing went on for quite some time I'm afraid to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your requests to see the rest of the camp were denied, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We said we wanted to interview more inmates because we had very little, apart from the obvious visual impressions from the canteen. One man coming up with the, for me, unforgettable line: "I do not want to tell any lies but I cannot tell the truth." And they started producing people for interview. One man in particular in the corridor as we made to -- we hoped, to look at the hangar, but in vain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I refused to talk to anyone. I said I refuse to talk to anyone that you produce. I want to be able to produce my interviewees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in that person that they wanted you to interview in the corridor was identified by way of a position?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: An official with the local SDA party which was the party in government in Sarajevo. Forgive me if it sounds brusque, but there was a -- it was a pretty antagonistic atmosphere by now, and they were suggesting people to interview and I decided that this -- that it wasn't worth talking to people who were presented by them to interview. We wanted to get on to the main business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they then take you to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, indirectly, yeah, we went out into the yard and spent a lot of time there continuing the arguments. And it was made clear that we weren't going to get into this hangar. At one point, the ITN fellow and I just walked towards Drljaca and Meakic who blocked our way with their guns, and this was -- we decided that we would go along with them at that point. It was not very nice. So yeah -- well, we wanted to stay, and they said: "Now we're going to Trnopolje because if you go into the hangar, you'll get behind on your schedule." So we eventually after quite an exchange, we agreed to continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. You always mention "they." If you could, please, be a little bit more concrete, to the best of your recollection, who was the person intervening or were the persons intervening at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly. Down in the yard when we were arguing and at this one rather risky point trying to get to the hangar, it was mostly Simo Drljaca, the chief of police, and the camp commander was also there, Meakic. And the conversations were translated by at this point in some instance from the ITN man from Belgrade but mostly Mrs. Balaban, and they were the people who were saying this. Major Milutinovic, too, was there, but it was mostly Mr. Drljaca who was preventing our progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With pleasure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you drove to the Trnopolje camp, tell us what your impressions were when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we were in a van and were going along. And to the left on the road was a remarkable sight, and we told the driver to stop. And he sort of didn't at first, but then did. And we just got out of the van. And across a scrap of land, the sight we saw was basically a fence, a barbed-wire fence, and behind it quite crowded, a group of men. And again, in various states of decay, but those who were in the serious state of decay were in a very serious state of decay, skeletal. And we made our way, myself and the ITN crew, across this scrap of land to the fence to introduce ourselves, present ourselves to this group of prisoners. Mutually amazed to see each other, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men that you spoke to behind the fence, did they indicate when they had arrived at the camp and from where?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of them had arrived at this place, Trnopolje, that very day. Some from Omarska, and others from a place of which I hadn't heard until then called Keraterm. And they had come that day from these places, and we started to ask about conditions both where we were now and where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these prisoners discuss any reluctance to discuss the conditions of their stay in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, some did, some didn't. Some were extremely scared because there were guards all around the place with guns listening to what was being said. I found it easier to talk when the cameras weren't pointing directly at them. The ITN translator was moving around, and I also managed to find a prisoner who spoke English. There was one man by the name of Alic who talked about a -- what he called a massacre. He said that -- he said then, I later met him and he said a different figure.
