He said then 200 people had been killed in one night in this place Keraterm, and that he had been asked to join a dispatch to clear up the bodies but that he had broken down, he couldn't do it and was replaced by another prisoner. I found this a shocking story. Others -- well, rather like Omarska really. If I can say, they spoke with their eyes. It's hard to describe this, or not. "No, I can't talk about it now." And after Omarska, I had become pretty used to the idea that with the guards around you had to do with this by intuition, by expression and then we were able to move around more freely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The massacre that you were told about that occurred in the Keraterm camp, did anyone identify the place in the Keraterm camp in any way where the massacre had taken place?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They said it was one of the hangars in the camp. I now know that it was called number 3, but I didn't find that out at the time. So they just said it was in a hangar. But I know more now than I did then, but I wasn't given the exact detail or location at that time, no. Not that I recall anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps now we could run a video taken by one of the ITN crews of about 27 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before we run it, again, Mr. Vulliamy, did you have anything to do with selecting what was filmed and how any film was edited or nonedited?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I was in a separate operation. A mere print journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before we begin, we also have the transcript of this video to hand out. It is video number 0000664. It's on the 65 ter list as -- we'll get that number. Number 804 on the 65 ter list. We would ask that the entire video and transcript be admitted once it's played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purposes of today, it should have the exhibit number DP3, and the transcript, DP3-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I do not want to misrepresent that this is the entire film, because it's not. We have so many selections from ITN, but this is one of them. It's about 27 minutes long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Journalist: We would really like to see it. "The Speaker: Or to Manjaca. "The Speaker: Why not? "The Speaker: They say, this is an investigation centre, so if they prove that they are guilty or not guilty, then there is a certain procedure. So this is a centre for investigation."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can we stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, can you identify the two men in uniform that we saw?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: On our left is Major Milutinovic, and on our right, chief of police, Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person in the shirt, in the screen in front of us gesturing, was that the interpreter that you're using?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: That's the interpreter contracted by ITN, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Journalist: That anyone could see it. The Red Cross couldn't come and now they're stopping us. We've seen nothing. We've seen one dining hall and 80 prisoners. "The Speaker: But we have a promise from Dr. Karadzic and now they're telling us something else."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could we stop the tape. I don't think we're starting at the beginning of the tape. It may not have been rewound. If we could rewind the tape entirely to the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it started with what we can read from the transcript. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, please. My fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please proceed with the video at the point we have just been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "The Journalist: We would really like to see it. "The Speaker: Or to Manjaca. "The Speaker: Why not? "The Speaker: This is an investigation centre, so if they prove that they are guilty or not guilty, then there is a certain procedure. So this is a centre for investigation. "The Journalist: Why can't we -- that anyone could see it. The Red Cross couldn't come and now they are stopping us. We've seen nothing. We've seen one dining hall and 80 prisoners. "The Speaker: All of them are going. "The Speaker: We cannot make a proper judgement about this camp until we see the way they live."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just stop a moment. Do you recall the name of the third person in uniform arriving now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's the camp -- I believe it's the camp commander, name of Meakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "The Speaker: Investigation centre, you can see how they eat. "The Speaker: We will have no other choice to say in our report that they did not fulfill Dr. Karadzic's promise and allow us to see what we wanted at this centre. "The Speaker: He said about security, about our because of our security. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "The Journalist: Further we will not be able to say on British television that this is not a concentration camp. "The Speaker: We have seen nothing yet. "The Speaker: Fighters. "The Speaker: Kozarac alone had 3500 armed people. "The Speaker: Are we going to Trnopolje or Banja Luka? "The Speaker: Banja Luka. "The Speaker: And your reason is? "The Speaker: What's your reason? "The Speaker: Just trying to do my best here. "The Speaker: Promised us something else, and said you can do this and this and that, and not that. If they say this is a protocol of your stay here, that will be all. I'm sorry. That will be all. "The Speaker: So he told you not to give us access to the majority of this camp. "The Speaker: I'm just translating. I'm just trying to do my best. "The Speaker: You now have a chance to go to Trnopolje. "The Speaker: Just a minute. "The Speaker: Yes. Yes, some security reasons are present here. "The Speaker: If you don't mind, you can go to Trnopolje or you can go to Banja Luka. I'm really sorry. I would like to do my best. Do you believe? "The Speaker: Access to this camp. We, all we have seen it 80 people having lunch. We can't judgement on the camp. "The Speaker: We would like five minutes in this building here. "The Speaker: But we also have some timetable for you here. "The Speaker: He is saying we are not safe. "The Speaker: Commander... Guarantee our safety. "The Speaker: Why can we not see five minutes in here? It's not going to throw our timetable out, five minutes looking in this building. "The Speaker: I'm sorry. It's not according to protocol. The protocol does not allow us to go there and... I'm sorry, really sorry, and that's all. "The Speaker: We're now being asked to leave this camp having seen nothing more than the canteen. We are being told that Dr. Karadzic's promise, while good to us, does not carry any weight here."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could stop the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All that we've seen so far is from the Omarska camp. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we'll proceed now, and can you identify when we next get to the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We could stop for a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this now, sir, the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah, this is Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Speaker: How are conditions for you here? How is the situation for you? "The Speaker: I don't know if I'm allowed to speak. "The Speaker: Is it difficult for you to speak? How long have you been here? "The Speaker: Before I came here. "The Speaker: Where did you come from? Did they take you from your home? "The Speaker: All from the same town? "The Speaker: From the surrounding of this town, the villages, and from our homes, yes. "The Speaker: Why did they say they were bringing you here? "The Speaker: Say us anything. "The Speaker: Why do you think you are here? Is it difficult for you here? "The Speaker: Yes. "The Speaker: How many of you are there here? "The Speaker: I'm not sure. I'm not quite sure about that. I just came today here. "The Speaker: Where were you before? "The Speaker: In another camp for 50 days, in the city. "The Speaker: Where are your families, your wives and children? "The Speaker: I don't know. We think they are home. I'm not sure. "The Speaker: Everybody is from Prijedor or close to Prijedor? "The Speaker: From the surroundings, from the villages around. "The Speaker: The Serbs say that you were, that you were fighters, that you were fighters with the Muslim forces. Is that right? "The Speaker: I'm not a fighter. I never fought. I've never fought. I don't know. "The Speaker: Can you tell me anything about the conditions in which you are being kept? Or is it difficult? "The Speaker: I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that, you know. Can you understand me? "The Speaker: How many times are you fed? How many times do you eat? "The Speaker: Before it was once upon a time once upon a day, once in a day, before, in the former camp. "The Speaker: And here? "The Speaker: I don't know. I just came here. We just came here today. "The Speaker: Are people here being beaten? "The Speaker: Here, no. Here, no, here. "The Speaker: But in other places? "The Speaker: I rather wouldn't talk about that, I'm not sure. "The Speaker: Thank you very much for speaking with us. We are from British television. This is the first time we have been able to -- we have known about your situation. This is the first time we were able to come and film you here. "The Speaker: It has taken us a long time to find you here, but we've, we wanted to find out what conditions you are being kept in or how things are for you here. "The Speaker: I was for two months in another place, and now I am here, they are saying we are going to go home soon from here. "The Speaker: How have things been in the other place? Can you tell us anything about the conditions that you have been kept in and the treatment of the people you were with? "The Speaker: Well, that was hard time. "The Speaker: We heard stories of people being beaten and people disappearing. Did that happen? "The Speaker: Well, I can't say much about that. See, people were hungry. "The Speaker: It was difficult? "The Speaker: It was difficult time, yes, for sure. "The Speaker: That's fine. And you have, you have just got here now today? "The Speaker: Yeah, we got here today. "The Speaker: Are the conditions better here? "The Speaker: Well, they are saying it's going be better here. People from here are supposed to go home. "The Speaker: And you are outside here in the sun? "The Speaker: Yeah, what can we do? "The Speaker: Do you know where all your family is? "The Speaker: Well, I know my wife, where she is, in Istra. And for other people, I don't know. "The Speaker: So you know your wife is, your wife is safe, your wife is...? "The Speaker: Yeah, my wife is safe. "The Speaker: So hopefully you will be able to join her soon. "The Speaker: Yeah. "The Speaker: I hope so. Because this is the first time that... "The Speaker: What are the conditions like in which you have been living in? "The Speaker: Conditions, very bad. "The Speaker: We don't have food or water. "The Speaker: Today? "The Speaker: We just came here today. "The Speaker: Where did you come from? "The Speaker: From Prijedor, Keraterm. "The Speaker: Prijedor. "The Speaker: What did they give you here to eat, to drink? "The Speaker: Nothing. "The Speaker: Here, tea and afternoon lunch, bread, and... "The Speaker: Soup. "The Speaker: Soup. "The Speaker: Someone was speaking English here? "The Speaker: Yes, I speak a little. "The Speaker: So for you, what have, what have the conditions been like since? How long have you been here held? "The Speaker: We came, we just came here. "The Speaker: From another camp. "The Speaker: From another camp. We don't about the condition here, except a little bit more better. "The Speaker: What was it like before? "The Speaker: It was terrible. We just eat two parts of bread and soup on the day. "The Speaker: The reason we are here, we've heard terrible stories about people. "The Speaker: Yeah. The story is very complicated here. You can translate it. It's the power. I think it's power of the arrest, arrest people, but this... "The Speaker: They don't give you anything to eat. "The Speaker: Have they told you how long you will be here? "The Speaker: They think perhaps next 20 days, rest, more people is here long time. Somebody goes very quick. I don't know. We just must, we must say here and wait with the rest. "The Speaker: Were you, were you interrogated at the last camp? "The Speaker: Pardon? "The Speaker: Were you interrogated at the last camp? Did they question you? "The Speaker: Personally, no, but the rest a little bit, more interrogated rest of the people. I have friends in England, Sweden, and some other parts, Germany. I'd like to say to all people that it isn't good any more. It's not life. "The Speaker: To form these camps. So we hope that when this is seen in, in Europe, it will help you all and it will mean that you will be, you'll be more quickly released. "The Speaker: I hope so. Yeah. "The Speaker: Anyway..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, is it correct from viewing that tape that there were certain prisoners within an area that was fenced off, and others outside?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The people who said that they had arrived there that day, who we initially saw, were in a different bit of the camp from the more sparsely distributed people that we saw on other bits of the film, yes, if that's what you were asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to some of these people that were outside the fenced-off area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Who were in the bit of the camp that was not fenced in?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I went in to the other bit of the camp with a young man who spoke English, a -- quite good English who showed me round during the time that we -- I had. And some of the time I spent with the ITN crew visiting what they called the medical facility and other bits of the camp that were not in the film, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not in the film we just showed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was cameras present when you went into the medical centre and met with Dr. Idriz Merdzanic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I was with the crew when they went to see the doctor, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you spoke to that were outside of the fenced area, did they indicate, any of them, indicate to you how they came to be in the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: They had come for a variety of reasons. Each that I spoke to, with their own story. Some had been marshalled from their homes, either because troops had arrived and rounded them up or because troop had arrived and attacked their houses or their villages, notably Kozarac but also others. And they had been marched there in columns under guard. Others had come of their own accord in flight, from their villages or towns, where their houses had been burned or shelled or had been shooting at them or at their houses. And they had come to seek, I suppose, what I saw at the time as being the protection of numbers. And my thought was if they fled to this, what have they fled from? But there were a variety of reasons. It was confusion in parts of that place, and there were a variety of reasons why people had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make any note of the sanitary conditions at the camp during your visit?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and they were bad. There were open latrines, open holes of excrement. It was very hot. There was little or no water, running water. The place was a converted school complex. It was rather bizarre because all of the paraphernalia of a school was on some of the walls. And I went inside to some of the sleeping quarters. Some were living indoors. Some were living out in the open. But the - my impression - I've got to be straight with this, is that it was not -- Omarska was the place that remained in my mind. It was bad, but not as bad. And I think I was sort of aware of that at the time. In fact, I know I was aware of that at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told that also by the prisoners behind the fence who said that they had arrived that day from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, it was clear from what they were saying and from what others were saying that I had interviewed from Keraterm and Omarska who had arrived that day that although it's rather perverse to say so, they were pleased to be there rather than where they had been before. I wouldn't say "pleased," sorry; relieved in comparison from whence they had come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the video, we saw an interview with a young man in a white T-shirt. You had indicated earlier that a lot of what you learned from was from what was not said. And I recall this man saying -- he was asked if there were beatings here, on page 9 of the transcript, he was asked, I believe by Mr. Williams, you can correct me if I am wrong, are people here being beaten? He said: "Here, no. No, here, not here." And the question about other places, he said: "I rather wouldn't talk about that. I'm not sure." Is that the kind of answer that gave you the impression that there was more information that the prisoners were reluctant to give?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Indeed. I didn't actually interview that particular man. But that's the sort of thing. Having now -- I would say this: It was in the canteen in Omarska where those -- I was conducting those sort of conversations. It was more painful to watch than that gentleman, this, as it were, articulate silence if that's what you mean or articulate reticence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We also saw on the video something being handed to someone behind the fence and a group quickly forming around them and people reaching in. Do you know what that was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I don't. But I would infer that it might be some sort of refreshment, water, food, bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any food or water handed to the people behind the fence while you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Very anxious to get to it, scrambling, but not violently, but certainly a scramble to get to whatever was being handed over the fence. Happened mainly when the cameras were around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, things were passed to them when the cameras were around. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was August the 5th of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: This is all August the 5th, yes. By the time we get to Trnopolje, it would have been mid-afternoon, mid to late afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left Trnopolje, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Back to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Belgrade, were you able to write a story and transmit it in some way to your newspaper?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we got to Belgrade late that night or in the early hours of the following morning. And I wrote and transmitted my article on the 6th of August, the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if ITN or Channel 4 broadcast tape from that visit on other the 5th or the 6th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I do know and did know that both were -- they went to Budapest to edit and send their material which was transmitted in the UK on the evening of August the 6th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your article would be published the 7th?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: The morning of the 7th, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe any reaction from the world press to the broadcasts and the publication concerning your visits to Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Well, yes. The 7th was quite a day because I was contacted by radio stations from all over the world. It went pretty berserk if you will forgive the expression. I was on -- I was taken down to the television studios in Belgrade. I was doing interviews all over the place. Indeed, there was quite a reaction. At the time -- everybody wanted to talk about concentration camps. At the time, I declined to use the term because of the connotations. I have since researched the term and it's history, not least in South Africa, so now I would use it. So, it was a big reaction, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any news organisation ask you to go back to the camp based upon those reports?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, for various complicated reasons to do with television franchise, partnerships and copyright, NBC, the American channel, were not able to transmit ITN's pictures because ITN was paired up with some other group in America. I can't remember which. So NBC was in a bit of a fix, and they wanted me to go and front, report on screen, their coverage of the follow up because I have to say Belgrade became quite a sort of bedlam of media during the aftermath of our story. And I don't mind calling it the media circus, it sort of descended on Trnopolje and NBC offered me quite a lot of money to go and do it for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you accept that and go back to the camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because, rightly or wrongly, there was a press conference in Belgrade given by vice-president Nikola Koljevic who, without -- I can't remember whether -- I think there was a list actually. But anyway, the gist of the press conference was: "We challenge the world, you, to go and look at the camps that we know about where Serbs are being held." And I had done the war in Croatia, and I had seen terrible things being done by both sides. And for reasons to do with -- well, I have to say professional, to keep, I mean, I spoke to my editor about this, and he said: "Well, let's keep ahead of the game. Let's keep ahead of the pack. You know, we have been to Omarska and Trnopolje. Now the circus is heading down there. Let's keep trying to set this agenda." And partly that, and partly because of my experience in Croatia where I had seen victims on both sides, I thought that the best thing to do was to head round to the other side, which I did, through Hungary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then visit a camp where Croatians were holding -- an area of Bosnia-Herzegovina controlled by Croatian forces where they were holding Serbs and publish an article concerning your visit there and the conditions in which the prisoners were held?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. And it took quite some effort, although slightly less effort than on the Serbian side. But eventually, with a colleague from the Associated Press, we managed to get into, partly by challenging them, saying: "Look, I was the person who the Serbs let into the camps where your people are being held," because there were Croatians in Omarska as well as Muslims, "what about yours?" And after the same sort of hassle, which I won't go into, we did manage to get inside a camp called Dretelj in which -- run by a Croatian militia called the HOS for Serbs. And while I now know, because I went -- never mind, I went back to it later when the Croatians were holding Muslims, I now know we didn't see the whole of that camp. I saw enough to see that the conditions were bad and very frightening for the prisoners. But most importantly, that contrary to what the Croatians were saying, women were being held in a warehouse there. And I published a story about this. But -- and -- one has to see these things on a scale, the conditions were very bad. They were worse than the camps we originally saw around Belgrade but incomparable [Realtime transcript read in error "comparable"] with Omarska and Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, is it correct, then, that at this camp in Croatian-controlled territory, Serbian women were being held prisoner?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I've just seen on my screen here that it says: "comparable with Omarska and Trnopolje." I said just the opposite, I said "incomparable with Omarska and Trnopolje." Excuse me,.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: By which I meant much much -- not as bad as Omarska and Trnopolje. Excuse me, I just saw that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just going back for a moment to your visit in the Omarska camp, you saw two or three groups going to lunch. Did you see, at any time, any women or were you shown any women during your visit to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: In Omarska, there were women working in the canteen, but as sort of kitchen staff. But I didn't see any women among the prisoners being drilled or eating. I now know differently, that there were women prisoners, but not at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about being in Belgrade after the publication of your story and the broadcast of the ITN and seeing the international press begin to descend - would it be correct - descend on Belgrade enroute to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct that following the publication of your stories, you observed members of the international press begin to move towards Prijedor from Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, very large numbers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just perhaps -- just before the break, I have a short videotape, the last one, showing the actual -- one of the broadcasts of ITN that motivated this. If we could play that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm only going to play the first broadcast, which I believe is about 7 or 8 minutes long, 8 minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please hear the ERN number, or if it already has an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's 0401, is the ERN number, in other words V000-0401. It's 65 ter number 825. It has not been exhibited yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the purposes of today, DP4. Please play the video now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: With sound, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Speaker: What else she saw in the camps. "The Speaker: Well, John, I have to say what we saw is enough. Enough to now make it absolutely essential that the Red Cross and the United Nations are given access to these camps in northern Bosnia as soon as possible. We left with serious misgivings about what's going on there, and with great suspicions that something very nasty is afoot. We went to two camps. One was a detention centre. We were taken in by the Serbian army under their protection and at their invitation. At the first detention centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could finish this after lunch. Because I think it's queued and I could be wrong. Okay proceed, I'm sorry again. I thought it was Mr. Williams' broadcast rather than Ms. Marshall. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Speaker: ... There is where the Muslim men are brought and they're interrogated and those that are found guilty of fighting are sent on we're told to a prison of war camp and those that aren't are sent on to a refugee camp. We saw terribly old men there, men paper thin, too terrified to speak to us. Terribly underfed, and only about 80 of a total Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of 1400 prisoners. We were not allowed to see the others. We were not allowed to see where they lived, what they were doing. In fact, we were escorted in the end away from the camp by men with guns and left with very, very grave doubts. At the second camp, some people there had come from this detention centre and from others, and then we heard very serious allegations, beatings, rapes, even shootings. We cannot verify them. We weren't in a position to check them out because we were under the escort of the people who were being accused, the side that was being accused of these crimes. We were able to smuggle out some photographs that do show some beating was going on. And we enough terror on the faces of these people to make it absolutely certain that this must be cleared up once and for all, the Red Cross must be allowed in. "The Speaker: These are the Muslim prisoners of Omarska. In small groups under heavy Serbian guard, they are ushered into the canteen for their single meal of the day. Most have been here for two months. They say they don't know why but they were rounded up from their homes. They were too frightened to talk about the way they have been treated, and the conditions in which they have been kept. Conditions which have been hidden from the world as the Serbs have denied access here to the United Nations and to the International Red Cross. Their prison is an old mining complex outside Banja Luka" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we stop for a moment, please. I just was informed there is no B/C/S interpretation. Is this correct, Dr. Stakic? Can you follow the video in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You are correct, there is no B/C/S translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No. Apparently, at least on this exhibit, there is not a transcript available. I can try to search, because the problem is we have some of this clip on many different videotapes, but I haven't seen a transcript associated with this particular videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the length of this clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's about 8 minutes long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 8 minutes long. Then I would ask that we proceed with this video, and take it in small portions and ask the interpreters to be so kind to do their very best in order to provide an interpretation for Dr. Stakic. This is mandatory, no doubt. The trial stays adjourned, or the deposition taking stays adjourned until 14.30. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Please be seated. The problem, has it been resolved regarding the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, thanks to the kind assistance of the court reporter we made a transcript, or she did, over the lunch hour of the tape, at about the point where we stopped it last time. That's an English transcript, but I believe it'll be of assistance to the booth. They all have it now, so they can do the translation from the transcript. I don't know if Your Honours want a copy, and the Defence also, of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Most important that Dr. Stakic has one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's in English. But the interpreters will be assisted by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Big thanks to everybody who provided us with this. And let's start and, please, give me a signal in case you can't follow because the video is too fast. Then let's stop immediately. I think we can start on this basis. Once again, the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The video is not now set for the very beginning, but for the point we stopped at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So this is the evidence available for this trial, from now on. Please start, with sound, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: "The Speaker: It's absolutely essential that the United Nations and the Red Cross are given access to these camps in northern Bosnia as soon as possible. We left with serious misgivings about what's going on there, and with great suspicions that something very nasty is afoot. We went to two camps. One was a detention centre, we were taken in by the Serbian army under their protection, and at their invitation. At the first Detention Centre, we were given very, very limited access, and this is where Muslim men are brought, and they are interrogated. And those that are found guilty of fighting are sent on we are told to a prisoner of war camp. And those that aren't are sent on to refugee --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I just asked for the tape to stop so the interpreters could catch up. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: "The Speaker: We saw terribly old men there. Men, paper thin, too terrified to speak to us, terribly underfed. And only about 80 of a total of 1400 prisoners. We were not allowed to see the others. We were not allowed to see where they lived, what they were doing. In fact, we were escorted in the end away from the camp by men with guns and left with very, very grave doubts. At the second camp, some people there had come from this Detention Centre and from others, and then we heard very serious allegations, beatings, rapes, even shootings. We cannot verify them. We weren't in a position to check them out because we were under the escort of the people who were being accused -- the side that were being accused of these crimes. We were able to smuggle out some photographs that do show some beatings going on. And we saw enough terror on the faces of these people to make absolutely certain that this must be cleared up once and for all. The Red Cross must be allowed in. "The Speaker: These are the Muslims prisoners of Omarska. In small groups, under heavy Serbian guard, they are ushered into the canteen for their single meal of the day. Most have been here for two months. They say they don't know why, but they were rounded up from their homes. There were two frightened to talk about the way they have been treated and the conditions in which they have been kept, conditions which have been hidden in the world as the Serbs have denied access here to the United Nations and to the International Red Cross. Their prison is an old mining complex outside Banja Luka in northern Bosnia. In an office above the canteen, the camp commandant and the spokeswoman for the local Serbian authorities said they have two and a half thousand of what they called internees who were being interrogated as possible Muslim fighters. "The Speaker: No, this is not a camp. This is a centre, a transit centre, Omarska and Trnopolje, both centres, not camps. "The Speaker: The prisoners were being brought to the canteen from a large industrial building in the centre of the mining complex. It, too, was under heavy guard, and we asked to be allowed to look inside. But in spite of promises of openness from the Serb Bosnian leader, Dr. Karadzic, we were told we could see no more. "The Speaker: Why are you not fulfilling Dr. Karadzic's promise to us? "The Speaker: He promised us something else, and said you could do this and this, and that and not that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Didn't we see this portion already?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last video that we saw was a rush video. It was raw footage, and this is the broadcast report containing portions of that rush footage and some other footage that we did not see from that camera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. [Videotape played]. "The Speaker: We are now being asked to leave this camp seeing nothing more than the canteen. We are being told that Dr. Karadzic's promise, while good to us, does not carry any weight here. As we were moved on, soldiers told us the army did not control the camp, which they said was will you know by the local authorities and militia. We had asked to be taken to a second camp, at Trnopolje, in the same area to which several hundred prisoners from Omarska had that day been transferred and which has also been at the centre of allegations of atrocities. Conditions at this camp were appalling. In 100 degree heat, hundreds of men were forced to eat and sleep outside in a field, behind barbed wire. Their meagre rations consist of a small hunk of bread and a bowl of soup every day. Here, too, they said they had been rounded up, whole villages emptied of their men. And they were afraid. "Can you tell me anything about the conditions in which you are being kept, or is it difficult? "I'm not sure that I'm allowed about that. "Can you understand me? "People here being beaten? "Here, no. Here, no. Not here. I rather wouldn't talk about that. I'm not sure. "Can you tell us anything about the conditions that you are being kept in and the treatment of the people you were with? "Well, that was hard time. What can you say? "We heard, we heard stories of people being beaten and people disappearing. Did that happen? "Well, I can't say much about that. "We just came here from another camp. And we didn't know what the condition here. We accept a little bit more better. "What was it like before? "It was terrible. "One of the prisoners asked us to check on him in several days' time to see that he hadn't been punished for speaking to us. And away from the camera there were allegations of routine beatings and executions. Several prisoners told us of retaliatory killings. In one instance, in which they claimed 150 of their fellow prisoners had been killed, following the death of ten Serbian soldiers in a Muslim village. We were told people had been beaten to death, and we were asked to smuggle a film out of the camp. The pictures show severe injuries apparently as a result of beatings. "In the makeshift medical centre, there were cases of scabies, malnutrition, and diarrhea. Local doctors said they were chronically short of medicine and drugs. Among them was a Muslim doctor. We asked him whether there had been any cases of beatings. "Many?" "On one side of the camp were refugees who were here simply because they had nowhere else to go, their homes having been destroyed. They have been told they can go as soon as they have a guarantee of a home outside Serb-controlled Bosnia. In Banja Luka, prisoners' wives have been queueing for days for the news of their men and to register as refugees because they, too, have nowhere to go. On the roads to Banja Luka, Muslim villages lie empty and deserted, homes destroyed. If there is eventually freedom for the men in the detention centres, it's unlikely to be in Serb-controlled Bosnia. Ian Williams, ITN, northern Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, that's the end of the portion of the tape that I wish in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just for clarification, I tried to follow in B/C/S. We saw this queue of persons lining up. Was this in which town, to the best of your recollection? Can you recall where this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the exact best of my recollection, that was in Prijedor, not Banja Luka. I take issue with the commentary on the film, that he has made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would this be identical with that you described earlier as this lining up in front of the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So far as I recognise it, it was that which we saw lining up outside the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, after this was broadcast, you indicated you were in Belgrade. Did you ever have occasion to speak to Mr. Koljevic following the broadcast and publication of your visit to Omarska and Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, we had tea together, English tea, at the Hyatt Hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Koljevic make any remarks concerning your visit to the camps that stick in your memory?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, made a rather barbed joke at, I suppose, my expense and at the expense of the media and the world, I suppose. He said -- he joked. He said: "So you found them." He said: "You'll do well out of this. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Took you a long time, didn't it?" And he chastised in a sort of semi-joking way, the concentration of the media and the world on the capital, the siege of the capital of Sarajevo, and he characterised this sympathy with "lovely old multiethnic city with its university being laid siege to by us barbarians," and he joked along these lines and made some remark like: "Of course there was no Winter Olympics in Prijedor. None of you ever took a holiday in Trnopolje." And well, we laughed for different reasons. I thought he probably had a point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he bring Venice into the story?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: And he said all this happening so near to Venice, a few kilometres down the road from Venice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to go back for a moment, you talked about visiting camps in which Serbian civilians were being held prisoner, in territory controlled by the HOS, Croatian militia. During that visit, did you receive something that you interpreted as a threat?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I received a threat from the commander of the camp and of the I think also of the -- one of the HOS units in this town near which the camp was called Capilinja. And we were pushing him on the presence of the women in the camp which we had been in the hut that had been sort of whisked past. And he said: "If you're a journalist, you're rather like a intelligence officer, the less you say, the longer you'll live." And I took that to mean don't mention the women. And I didn't think that my life was in danger, one doesn't when people make these threats. Got used to them. But it was a menacing enough remark, and I was on my way back to Zagreb, and I was fairly wary of them perhaps knowing where I was because, I did, of course, write about the women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in writing about the women in that camp, did you also, in fact, even publish that threat and name the major, the Croat officer, who had threatened you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I'm sure I published the threat. I don't remember the man's name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it Major Miro Hrstic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that rings a bell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, in your experience in covering wars in Bosnia, was there a danger to journalists in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: There was certainly a danger to journalists in Bosnia. I think some 42 were killed, mostly from the local agencies and press. But some from outside the area as well, and I was myself involved in the retrieval of a body of one of them, BBC cameraman, a Croat in Central Bosnia. We went up to get it with a unit from the Croatian army. He had been killed by a tank round, a Serbian tank round, while driving his vehicle clearly marked "press."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your visit, your article, about Serbian civilians detained in camps controlled by the HOS, did you return to Prijedor on the 17th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. With a specific motive, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that visit, did you have -- first, did you have official permission from Republika Srpska authorities for that visit, as you did --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the background, what motivated you to go back to the opstina, the municipality of Prijedor, on the 17th of August?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I came back from the HOS camp to Zagreb, and immediately on arrival there had to report the story of a decision by the Croatian government to close their border to the by now stream, I would say a flood, of refugees and deportees coming across their borders, mostly at Karlovac which I mentioned earlier. But other places, too. Croatia had by then become a young nation, but one basically full of refugees and deportees. And I remember reporting the government saying they now had 600.000 people from Bosnia and they just couldn't take any more. So they closed their border to any more. And we were talking about, a colleague and I, were talking about this in Zagreb, and I can't exactly remember who said what to who. But I mean the gist of it was well, that's the front door shut. But I'm sure they are not or we were sure they weren't going to stop deporting people. So we had better find out where they are going and where the back door is. And I remember with some trepidation, it dawned on us that the only way to find out was to get, to use the expression, to get ethnically cleansed ourselves and to find out from the inside where people were being deported to. And the way of doing that was to cross over from Croatia, across an area of Croatia under Serbian control, and into the Serbian bit of Bosnia, which was then called the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With whom and by what means did you travel?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Travelled in a rental car with a colleague called Andre Gustincic [phoen] from Reuters, who was a Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I presume because he spoke the language you did not have an interpreter with you? Was it just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, indeed, we were later joined by a reporter from the AP, the Associated Press, called Maud Beelman. But to put it frankly, I'd worked with Andre Gustincic [phoen] a lot in the past and in Croatia, and he didn't have a driving license. And the deal was I drove and he translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no interpreter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No, there was no interpreter. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the surroundings of Prijedor did you actually go?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Went to Prijedor. I think we asked -- we actually made a brief pass by the civic centre. I can't remember why, a briefing from the police or something. But we were sent on our way. And we then started out down the road towards -- in the direction of Banja Luka and familiarly enough past the sign to Omarska. And saw a sight which was -- I mean, simultaneously, it was gratifying from I suppose from a professional point of view of why we were there, but it was otherwise pretty depressing. An extraordinary large convoy of mostly cars, some buses, and trucks parked alongside the road. Long convoy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to any of the persons in this convoy and learn where they were from and where they were headed, if they knew?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. We -- well, we slipped into the convoy. We found a space in it, and put our car into it. And of course started talking to the people. They were from a town called Sanski Most to the south of Prijedor and they had been marshalled that morning, after quite a -- as they reported, a considerable amount of violence against their homes. And they said that they had been told to assemble, that they were to leave the town in the convoy. But for the most part, at least initially when we spoke to them, they did not know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any police or army escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. There were armed guards, so far as I could tell, mostly from the police, civilian, units, not in green camouflage but in blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall if it was the light blue police shirt or if it was a camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: As I recall, it was a light blue police tunic, shirt, uniform, but I think some of them had darker blue sort of anoraks or jackets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd now like you to recount for us the journey that you took with this group of people. I'm going to try not to interrupt you, and tell us what it was like to be on one of these convoys of persons going from the Krajina area to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: You mentioned Travnik, and indeed, some people further -- later in the day, further along the line did have some idea that we might be going to Travnik. I had never heard of the place. It became increasingly confusing and terrifying as it went along. We started out down the road. They had pulled over on the side of the road when we found them for what we later learned was one of a number of stops or pauses or marshalling to order along the route. We went through Banja Luka and took a sort of turning off the main road, which started to climb towards hillier terrain. There were various stops. I can remember one man's car broke down, and I'll never forget the terror on his face when he thought that he might perhaps be abandoned without the protection of numbers in this increasingly hostile terrain. They quickly attached a rope to his car so that he could be pulled. This was the car in front of us, in fact. We went through a town called Skender Vakuf where I was stopped actually. And a guard, a soldier, who had had a few drinks started talking to me. And I was pretty scared because I didn't want to give myself away as a foreigner. So I pretended to be deaf and dumb. I just went like this. And Andre said: "He's from Australia. It's all a mistake." And this man gave me a Chinese burn on my arm and a bit of a kick through the door, wrenched the windscreen wiper off the car, kicked the door shut, and then we went on. That was the sort of atmosphere. We saw an awful lot of, from my point of view very interesting, because it was a rare view of the guns, of the Serbian gun positions above -- atop the hills. And you could see that they -- perhaps not relevant here it was very interesting to see how much hardware that was up there and plentiful ammunition. But everywhere there were trucks and people giving the Serbian salute at our convoy and spitting and shouting. And then we got to a place called Vitovlje, and I can remember the people running across the fields and gardens of the village, shouting a term which Andre told me meant: "Slaughter them, slaughter them." Using a word - and I don't know, because I don't know the language, but Andre said - which was supposed to apply to animals, not people. And then it got dark, or started to get dark. We pull over again at a sort of factory farm or chicken hut. And one of our party, the lady from the AP, said: "Oh, is this the final destination?" Is this going to be -- should we be mentioning the unmentionable? You know, is this a camp or are they going to kill us? We didn't know what the hell was going on or where we were going. By the time we left Vitovlje, we were skirting mountain passes, and as dusk fell, we could hear, in the bushes beside the road, guns and shooting over the top of the convoy. Then there was a final stop, penultimate stop before the end, when they went down the convoy which was by now we counted and we estimated 58 cars, some 8 or so buses and trucks. Calculated about 1600 people in all. The -- they went down the convoy, it appeared, taking property. They did not take ours. We decided that this was the point at which it was advisable to declare that we were with the press. They did take our petrol, gas, but they were moving down the convoy. Then we moved on. And by now, there was more shooting. And I don't think that was at us or over us. I think this was part of the exchange of fire where we were getting to, which was the front line. A place called Smet. And by now, the police had -- the people that had escorted us to this far had gone back to Prijedor and we were now in the hands of a different lot of people, some irregulars, and others in a sort of paramilitary uniform. And the -- they basically took all the cars. They yanked the people out of the cars at gunpoint, and some were able to marshal belongings from the car, but not as I recall from the trunks of the cars. And the cars were driven away. And the convoy -- we weren't. We actually managed to chat to the people at the checkpoint, and Andre and I, we were joking about the Belgrade soccer team and we were sort of quite anxious to ingratiate ourselves with these people. So they said you can take your car through. We then packed it full of people and people on top, as well, and I knew that we were now starting to -- we were doing what you never and I know you never do which is cross lines in a war. Never, never cross the lines. Rule number 1. And the convoy set off into the night on foot, apart from us and I think a couple of other cars which for some reason were allowed to... We got to a pile of rocks in the road which was the demarcation between the two territories. There was a drop on one side, at least a bit of grass and a drop, and clearly mines around the rocks. So we left the car obviously and joined this clamber over the rocks. If you can imagine all these people climbing over the rocks, there were children there, very old people. I remember a man in a wheelchair having to be taken out of the chair going over and a man coming over. There was teddy bears and then, it was just anybody. But once over the rocks, we were in the battlefield basically. And down below was a village which I now know to be called Kozice or something. And they were shelling that village, and there was recent but not immediately shed blood on the road, and there had obviously -- well, there were the signs of mortar, mortar attacks or mortar fire because there were -- there was -- well, I stepped on a body part on the road. There had clearly been fighting, serious fighting, in that area. We carried on. We were marshalled by an enterprising man into a single-file line as far apart as was feasible because if a mortar hit us, then that would minimize the casualty. And we carried on. I mean, the whole thing took about 14 hours. And I will not forget things like a man shuffling forward in his slippers, and I talked Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to him. And I later learned that he died. We were then -- because the fighting was quite heavy in the valley, we were told to go up a mountain. I didn't know then, I knew nothing then, but I now know it to be called Mount Vlasic. And then down the other side. And that's where the first people from the Bosnian army, the government army, met up at a place called Turbet, and a young man said: "We have buses to take you the rest of the way. Welcome to Travnik." And I'll never forget the woman touching the thing on his arm, very relieved, I suppose, to be there. And that night we arrived in a place I had never heard of called Travnik. It had been a very long day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following that journey, did you on any occasion attempt to get permission while the war was still going on to re-enter the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: When I say "many," I mean between five and ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get official permission to re-enter Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. A couple of times I got as far as Pale from Sarajevo, but permission was declined by the woman in charge of press accreditation, who was actually Dr. Karadzic's daughter Sonja. I was not granted permission to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back for a moment to the video where we saw the women in line, you indicated that that was in Prijedor outside the municipal building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: F well, if it wasn't, it was very, very similar to what we saw in Prijedor. I don't think that was Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that line of women visible from the front entrance of the Municipal Assembly building --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, right opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be possible that the competent unit provide us, until tomorrow, with a still of this picture that we can identify the buildings around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll do that, or I may try to find it in a video that shows more surroundings. I think there's a video that shows more of the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to move on now. You indicated that you were reassigned to Washington, and then came back later at the very end of the war in 1995 with an assignment to write some retrospective series about untold stories of the war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been February 1994. I was pretty much instructed by my paper to leave Bosnia. They -- my editors decided I had been doing this too long. I wanted to stay but they took me out. Went to America, and I asked to come back to -- yeah, become the first U.S. bureau chief to be asked to be transferred to the Balkans. It was at my request that I returned. And I was based in London, and I covered the conclusion of the war from, I suppose, early summer 1995, the fallout from Srebrenica, and the NATO bombing which ended the war. And then sat down with my editor, the foreign editor, by now a new foreign editor who said well this is the conflict was what it is. We didn't think that the whole story by any means had been told. And he commissioned me to research what were going to be -- what was going to be a series of long articles and which were going to try -- well, in which I would retrace my steps and retrace some of the steps of the war and of the diplomatic shenanigans, to try and tell and illuminate the background to what had been in the news week in, week out for years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In February 1996, did you return to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, did you interview or attempt to interview several individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to go back to Omarska, and I wanted to seek out and interview the people that we had met before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the -- try to go to the Omarska camp in February 1996? And this is just to remind us, after Dayton. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, all this is after the end of the war, and the war ended by the Dayton agreement. And indeed, with a colleague, I went to Omarska, to the former camp, a mine again now. First time certainly I had had the opportunity to have a proper look at it, at its location and whereabouts. And there were three guards there at the entrance, this time the front entrance. And they did not allow us to go in, but we did talk to them, and they said that there had been no camp there and it was all lies. And we talked about the pictures and they said it was a montage, this sort of conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask them their names?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, and they refused to give them, making a reference to this Tribunal actually. They said a man called Tadic had been arrested and had been brought here, and I knew about that because I had actually been interviewed about it before by the Tribunal. And -- well, not about him but about the camps. And they said: "Oh, no names, please. We've had a nice conversation, but no names. You never can tell." They took Dule Tadic to The Hague, and they said that they knew him and he had a nice cafe and so on. It was like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the people that you interviewed in February of 1996, did you interview Dr. Milan Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, where was it that you -- how did you get in contact with Dr. Kovacevic and where did you interview him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: We interviewed him at his work which was the Prijedor hospital of which he was the director and found out that he was the director. If you will pardon, I'll explain. In Banja Luka, the night after we had been to Omarska and endeavoured to speak to Mr. Drljaca, without success, a translator, Serbian-speaking translator, was working with another colleague, and we happened to meet up in a restaurant and were talking about what we were -- what we were hoping to do. And it was this person who knew where Dr. Kovacevic was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we" spoke to, was there any other journalist with you on this trip?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: His name was Roger Cohen [phoen]. He works for the New York Times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Besides yourself and Mr. Cohen [phoen], was there an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. We wanted this individual to accompany us because he/she was particularly sort of knowledgeable and experienced. But she was unavailable because was working with somebody else, and recommended somebody who she regarded as competent. And he was in Bijeljina and called him and came down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately what time of day was it that you interviewed Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this occur in some type of office?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It was in his office at the hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, without referring to any notes at the moment, just what you recall now six years later what you recall about that conversation? And later, we can go over your notes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: I recall him being fairly haunted by it all. He produced a bottle of homemade brandy from a cupboard and drank a quantity of it. And to summarise, his discourse was a mixture of remorse, a fairly haunted sort of - how can I say? - outburst in a way of bitterness over what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think it would be best for you to read your shorthand notes to recollect as much as possible the details of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's up to the Court. I mean, I can go into more detail from memory if the Court wishes. I remember it pretty well, but it's absolutely up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We all know that witness evidence, please, don't take it personally, witness evidence is in most cases the worst evidence. And therefore, based on personal notes, yes, they no doubt, there can be additional probative value. I think it would be advisable that these notes be distributed to the parties. And as far as I understand, this should be under seal, the remaining pages, for which special reasons, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, these are personal notes. I'm going to ask the witness also about a conversation with Dr. Stakic. So I'd ask him to go through these and tell us if these notes that I have contain the interviews of 1996 with Drs. Kovacevic and Stakic and ask him if there's any other material that he does not want to be disclosed publicly. And if so, let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So let's proceed this way. The usher please give one copy first to the witness, and before we proceed, may be provided to everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you finished?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: It's fine, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't have a problem of this being disclosed publicly, to the Defence, to the accused?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it may be distributed, please, to the Defence and to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While it's being distributed, a few questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your normal practice in taking notes during an interview to include the question? Or would that normally not be something that you write down?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: Normally not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, was it your practice when you covered the wars in the Former Yugoslavia to bring a tape recorder to the field, or did you have any audiorecording equipment normally with you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD SEBASTIAN VULLIAMY
utterances.text: No. I had one, but it was stolen at a roadblock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, I think we are all prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No, unfortunately not. So please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I think we can proceed now, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We can proceed. I think as to the fact that this is more or less a loose leaf collection, we have to take care that we all have the document in the same order.
